AImonks () is an AI-Educational Publication. # *When Accuracy Isn’t Enough: The Case for Perturbation Testing in Machine Learning*. ## Abstract. * **Context:** Machine learning models often excel in clean test environments but fail under real-world data noise or shift. * **Problem:** Traditional evaluation metrics overlook model fragility when inputs change slightly. * **Approach:** We apply perturbation testing to assess robustness using noise injection and feature masking. * **Results:** Accuracy dropped from 96.5% to 91.2% under noise, revealing hidden sensitivity. * **Conclusion:** Perturbation tests expose brittleness and should be standard in model validation pipelines. **Keywords**: perturbation testing; model robustness; medical AI; sensor data drift; adversarial resilience. ## What If the Real World Is the Adversary? In 2020, a healthcare AI model deployed to predict COVID-19 patient deterioration in emergency rooms across multiple hospitals failed unexpectedly. Switching from absolute numbers to categorical bins was A harmless change in how oxygen saturation was recorded. Once praised for its cross-hospital accuracy, the model began misclassifying high-risk patients as low-risk. Models can’t just be accurate; they must be **resilient**. And that resilience must be **deliberately tested**. Enter perturbation testing [1–5]. ## Published in 𝐀𝐈 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐤𝐬.𝐢𝐨. ·Last published 1 day ago. results.title: Robustness tests for biomedical foundation models should tailor to specifications | npj Digital Medicine
results.content: # Robustness tests for biomedical foundation models should tailor to specifications. Our approach facilitates the standardization of robustness assessments in the model lifecycle and connects abstract AI regulatory frameworks with concrete testing procedures. Robustness1.") is an equally important topic, which generally refers to the consistency of model prediction to distribution shifts. Robustness failures are an origin of the performance gap between model development and deployment, performance degradation over time, and, more alarmingly, the generation of misleading or harmful content by imperfect users or bad actors2."). **c** Specification of robustness by a simplified threat model (defined by a distance bound) or priority (defined by realistic artifacts) in the task domain, shown with two examples. **Interventional robustness** refers to the invariance of model behavior to causally-defined interventions (e.g., image background or contrast shift, patient age shift) that characterize distribution shifts. **Out-of-distribution robustness** is a model’s resistance to semantic or covariate shift of test examples from the training data distribution. **Feature & Data robustness** define the robustness concepts based on the model performance change by removing or adding specific features or data in model development. **Development-stage robustness** resists corruption during model development by noise in labels or data, or by adversarial attacks with poisoning and back-door attacks as the most common examples. **Group robustness** refers to the resistance of model performance against subpopulation distribution shifts. **Longitudinal robustness** refers to the consistency of model performance against temporal shifts or nonstationary effects in the data distribution. Testing group robustness may modify subpopulation labels in patient descriptions to gauge the change in model performance20."). Robustness tests against aleatoric uncertainty may assess the sensitivity of model output to prompt formatting and paraphrasing, while assessing robustness to epistemic uncertainty may use out-of-context examples21. Specifying and testing robustness for more complex AI systems should also account for performance tradeoffs, model architectures, and user interactions. Existing health information technology regulations, such as the US-based HTI-1 final rule by the Office of the National Coordinator, focus primarily on transparency and disclosures of the use of predictive decision support models, yet lack detailed robustness requirements. For model developers, robustness testing informs model selection and updates. *et al.* Robustness tests for biomedical foundation models should tailor to specifications.

results.title: Monotonicity Constraints — Using Driverless AI 1.10.7.5 documentation
results.content: Monotonicity can be enforced for the feature engineering pipeline, the fitted model(s), or the entire modeling pipeline. Monotonicity constraints enforce a monotonic relationship between a specified feature and the target prediction. When monotonicity constraints are enabled, Driverless AI automatically determines if monotonicity is present and then enforces it through all or part of the modeling pipelines. Depending on the level of correlation between a feature and the target, Driverless AI assigns positive, negative, or no monotonicity constraints. To build an **entire monotonic gbm modeling pipeline** with a single click, user can select the monotonic\_gbm recipe from the Experiment settings of the expert panel. Driverless AI will automatically adjust multiple settings so that monotonicity is enforced on the feature engineering and model building level. For details see Monotonic GBM in pipeline building recipe under experiment expert settings. For more granular control, over thresholds, manual override of monotonicity constraints etc, refer to these settings under feature settings of the expert panel of an experiment. To build monotonic fitted models, ensure that:. * The Interpretability setting for the experiment must be greater than or equal to the monotonicity\_constraints\_interpretability\_switch, that has a default value of 7). So Interpretability setting for the experiment and/or `monotonicity_constraints_interpretability_switch` can be toggled to achieve this. * The final model must be linear (for example, GLMModel) or otherwise support monotonic constraints (LightGBMModel, XGBoostGBMModel, XGBoostDartModel or Decision Tree models). These can be set to ‘ON’ from the Model settings of the expert panel. See monotonicity constraints drop low correlation features. This can be toggled under experiment settings of the expert panel. and for monotonic feature engineering:. * Disable features engineered from multi-feature interaction i.e set max\_feature\_interaction\_depth to 1 in feature settings under expert settings panel. * Disable numerical to categorical feature transformations i.e set num\_as\_cat to False in the feature settings under expert settings panel. * For numeric features, allow only monotonic transformations i.e set included\_transformers to [‘OriginalTransformer’] only under recipe settings of the expert panel. The following table lists an example of settings to create a monotonic Driverless AI modeling pipeline. To enable entire monotonic gbm modeling pipeline with a single click see monotonic\_gbm recipe in pipeline building recipe under experiment expert settings.

results.title: Feature Engineering in MLOps: From Raw Signals to Smarter Models | by Kim Boher | Medium
results.content: # Feature Engineering in MLOps: From Raw Signals to Smarter Models. 🎯 **Feature Engineering** — the art of turning raw data into meaningful signals for machine learning. ## 🧠 What Is Feature Engineering? Feature engineering is the process of extracting, transforming, and selecting key attributes (features) from raw data to help machine learning models learn better and generalize effectively. Rather than feeding raw signals directly into your model, you shape them to emphasize what’s relevant. ## 🧰 Who Owns Feature Engineering? Feature engineering typically sits with **ML researchers and engineers**, but it depends on the workflow:. Feature engineering connects the well-prepared dataset to the model-building phase, and it plays a pivotal role in performance, accuracy, and deployment viability. 1. **Input** — capturing the raw audio signal. 2. **Preprocessing** — transforming the audio (e.g., into spectrograms or MFCCs). If your MFCC model burns power and crashes your microcontroller, it’s useless — even if it has 90% accuracy in a notebook. 👉 Your **ML engineer must balance performance with deployment constraints**. ## 🏗 Feature Stores: Organizing the Signal. To streamline and scale feature engineering, modern MLOps pipelines use **feature stores**. 📦 **Feature Store** = A centralized layer that stores, shares, and reuses engineered features across teams and models. ## 🧪 Best Practices for Feature Engineering in MLOps. 1. **Understand your sensor** — Features should reflect device behavior (e.g., microphone characteristics). 2. **Measure trade-offs** — Always test latency, power, and memory alongside accuracy. 4. **Monitor drift** — Feature distributions can shift over time in the real world. 5. **Version everything** — Store feature sets alongside training configs. Feature engineering is not just about squeezing performance from your model — it’s about understanding the **fundamentals** of your data, hardware, and use case. In a world where models are deployed on everything from phones to toasters, your ability to **extract the right features** can be the difference between a smart product and a silent one. > *🎯 Models learn from what you feed them. > Feed them features, not noise.*. Feature engineering is the often-overlooked heartbeat of production-ready machine learning. 💬 Let’s connect — or feel free to DM me.
